Hi Maren, glad it's useful. I can't place a CTEM episode, so I'm not sure which one you mean. Short answer: time-to-first-report is still my anchor. Continuous exposure programs add more signals, but the human reaction speed is still the n

disclosed.text: measure from the moment the attack reaches the person (the delivery or call time) to the first report, whichever channel they use. Mail, ticket or hotline are just entry points. The owner should be your triage team, not the reporter, so the clock can't be gamed.
as few people as possible. Nobody outside triage should be able to edit the timestamp. Others can read it, and any exception should be logged and approved.
the triage/security team owns the clock, everyone else gets read access, and exceptions are approved by the security lead and logged
I look at the median time to first report across the whole group, not at individuals, and I never publish names.
Triage proposes, a second function (security lead or works council rep) co-signs, and every exception is logged with a reason and reviewed quarterly.

Read the log with the security lead and a neutral second person. A works council rep works well for that. Treat it as a process problem when the same cause shows up in more than one site or quarter, or when the share keeps rising over two quarters.

the one-tap should create the report with the timestamp already set and assign it automatically to the triage on-duty rota, never to a person. If nobody acknowledges within a set window, it escalates to the triage lead.

keep one queue but two clocks. The reporting clock stays the SLA for human reports. Exposure signals get priority only when they are confirmed as actively exploitable or hit a critical asset. Then triage lead decides and logs the override, same as any exception.
I'd put it with the triage lead, since they own the SLA, and the SOC shift plan just feeds them who is on duty. Whoever owns it should be one named role, not a team.
when the triage lead logs their own override, the co-sign should come from someone above the lead, such as the security lead. The neutral second person reads the log at the quarterly review.
make 'above the lead' a fixed named role, not a person. The lead triggers the co-sign at the time of the override, and the quarterly log review then checks that none were skipped.
make it a fixed role by title, such as the security lead. The neutral second person who reads the log can also do the quarterly review, as long as they are independent of triage
